sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match or one word).

questions.q: (a) Name the physical quantity whose SI unit is V m. (b) A neutral pith ball is connected by a copper wire to a negatively charged rod. What charge does it acquire?
Fill in the blanks: (a) Electric potential is a ______ quantity. (b) A ring of radius R carries charge q; the field at its centre is ______.
Fill in the blanks: (a) The total flux through a closed surface is ______ times the charge enclosed. (b) Electric field lines never ______ each other.
State True or False: (a) A dipole in a uniform field experiences no net force. (b) Charge is quantized.
questions.answer:
(a) True — only a torque.
(b) True — q = ne.

questions.q: Spheres A (+2Q) and B (−Q) attract with force F. They are touched and replaced. (a) Charge on each = ______. (b) New force = ______.
questions.answer:
(a) (2Q − Q)/2 = +Q/2 each.
(b) k(Q/2)²/r² = kQ²/4r² = F/8, now repulsive (F = 2kQ²/r²).

questions.q: Give one word: (a) The unit of electric dipole moment. (b) The field of a dipole on its axis varies as 1/r to the power ______.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Define electric dipole moment. Give its SI unit.
questions.answer: The product of either charge and the distance between them, p = q × 2a, directed from −q to +q. SI unit: coulomb metre (C m).

questions.q: How does an electric dipole behave in a non-uniform electric field?
questions.answer: The forces on its two charges are unequal, so it feels a net force (it moves towards the stronger field when aligned) as well as a torque that tends to align it with the field.

questions.q: The electric flux through a Gaussian surface is zero. Does it mean that (a) the charge enclosed is zero and (b) the field is zero everywhere on the surface?
questions.answer:
(a) Yes — by Gauss's theorem φ = q/ε₀, so the net charge enclosed is zero.
(b) Not necessarily — field lines may enter and leave, giving zero net flux even where E ≠ 0 (e.g. a surface near an outside charge).

questions.q: Draw graphs showing how E and V vary with distance r from the centre of a uniformly charged spherical shell of radius R.
questions.answer:
E: zero for r < R, maximum at r = R, then falling as 1/r² outside.
V: constant (= q/4πε₀R) inside and on the shell, then falling as 1/r outside.

questions.q: Why is the test charge taken very small (q₀ → 0) when defining the electric field?
questions.answer: A large test charge would exert forces on the source charges and disturb their positions, changing the very field being measured. Taking q₀ → 0 ensures the field measured is that of the source alone.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Two large plane sheets with charge densities σ and −2σ are parallel and a distance d apart. Find the field (a) to the left of the first sheet, (b) to the right of the second and (c) between them.
questions.answer:
Each sheet gives E = |σ|/2ε₀, away from a positive sheet and towards a negative one. Take +x to the right.
(a) Left: σ sheet gives σ/2ε₀ to the left; −2σ sheet gives σ/ε₀ to the right. Net σ/2ε₀ to the right.
(b) Right: σ/2ε₀ to the right and σ/ε₀ to the left. Net σ/2ε₀ to the left.
(c) Between: σ/2ε₀ + σ/ε₀ = 3σ/2ε₀, towards the −2σ sheet.

or.q: Show that a dipole p at angle θ to a uniform field E experiences a torque τ = p × E.
or.answer:
Forces +qE and −qE are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero, but they form a couple.
Torque = force × perpendicular distance = qE × 2a sin θ = pE sin θ.
In vector form τ = p × E; it tends to align p with E.

questions.q: What are electric field lines? State three properties. Draw them for a single positive charge and for a dipole.
questions.answer:
Field lines are imaginary curves whose tangent at any point gives the direction of the field there.
Properties: (1) they start on positive and end on negative charges; (2) two lines never cross; (3) they are dense where the field is strong; (4) they meet a conductor's surface at right angles.
Positive charge: straight lines pointing radially outward. Dipole: lines curve from +q round to −q.

questions.q: Show that the electric field of a short dipole at a point on its perpendicular bisector varies inversely as the cube of the distance.
questions.answer:
At distance r on the bisector, each charge is √(r² + a²) away, with field kq/(r² + a²).
The components along the bisector cancel; the components parallel to the axis add: E = 2kq a/(r² + a²)^(3/2) = kp/(r² + a²)^(3/2).
For a short dipole (a ≪ r): E = p/4πε₀r³, so E ∝ 1/r³ (directed opposite to p).

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: State Gauss's theorem. Use it to find the field due to (a) an infinite plane sheet of charge and (b) a uniformly charged spherical shell at points outside and inside.
questions.answer:
Gauss's theorem: the total electric flux through any closed surface = q_enclosed/ε₀.
(a) Plane sheet (σ): take a cylinder through the sheet. Flux passes only through the two end faces: 2EA = σA/ε₀ ⇒ E = σ/2ε₀, uniform and independent of distance.
(b) Shell (charge q, radius R):
Outside (r > R): a sphere of radius r gives E × 4πr² = q/ε₀ ⇒ E = q/4πε₀r², as if all the charge were at the centre.
Inside (r < R): no charge is enclosed ⇒ E = 0.

questions.q: Define electric field at a point. Explain field lines and derive the field due to a dipole on its axial line.
questions.answer:
Electric field E = F/q₀ (q₀ → 0), the force per unit positive test charge; unit N/C or V/m.
Field lines show the direction of E, start on + and end on − charges, and never cross.
Axial field at distance r from the centre of a dipole (±q, 2a apart): E = kq/(r − a)² − kq/(r + a)² = kq × 4ar/(r² − a²)².
For a short dipole (a ≪ r): E = 2p/4πε₀r³ along p.
